node.label: Philip Curtin
node.date_label: The Image of Africa (1964) · The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969) · Cross-Cultural Trade in World History (1984) · On the Fringes of History: A Memoir (2005)
node.description: A historian of Africa, forced migration and cross-cultural connections who combined quantitative reconstruction with comparative world history. Joseph C. Miller’s substantive memorial describes how the slave-trade census grew from a question about regional economic context and how its estimate prompted further archival work. The same account identifies recurring global subjects such as trade, plantations, migration and disease. The entry preserves uncertainty and the distinction between counting a forced migration and explaining enslaved people’s lived experience; it does not adopt a historical estimate as a current audited total.

The 1964/1965 discrepancy is explicit, and the contemporary bibliography supports 1964.

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes source criticism and estimation central to reconstructing the scale of the Atlantic slave trade.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Joseph C. Miller’s 2009 account of the census’s origin, uncertainty and later archival responses. No fresh reading of the census or audit of modern SlaveVoyages totals; counting is not a substitute for enslaved experience.

proposed_edges.relationship: Develops comparative questions around recurring cross-cultural trade, migration, plantations and disease.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Miller’s substantive account supplies the methodological characterization; the publisher record supports title/date only. A specific comparative agenda, not the claim that one historian founded all global history or a causal affiliation arrow.
